problems.statement: One hundred apples are packed into twelve boxes. What is the largest number n for which you can always be sure that some box holds at least n apples?

choices.misconception: I divided 100 by 12 and rounded down instead of up.
I rounded the division to a convenient number without checking that a packing with a smaller maximum exists.
I gave the number of boxes as the answer rather than a number of apples.
I described the case where one box holds everything, which is possible but not guaranteed.

hints: Look at the fullest box.
Suppose every box held fewer than n. Work out the largest total that would allow, and find the smallest n making that total fall short of 100. Then build a packing that reaches exactly n.
If every box held at most 8 the total would be at most 96, short of 100 - so some box holds at least 9. And 9 is achievable: four boxes of 9 and eight of 8 make exactly 100.

solutions.reliable: Both halves are needed. First the bound: if every box held 8 or fewer, the total would be at most 12 x 8 = 96, which is less than 100 - so some box must hold at least 9. Then the example: four boxes of 9 and eight boxes of 8 add to 36 + 64 = 100, and no box holds more than 9. So 9 is guaranteed and 10 is not. The transferable idea: an always question needs a bound and a matching example, and only the two together pin the answer down.
solutions.elegant: The fullest box holds at least the average rounded up, which is 100 divided by 12 rounded up - that is 9.

problems.whyOnTest: Looking at the extreme object rather than a typical one is the whole method, and the answer is the average rounded up rather than down.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The numbers 1 to 10 stand in a row. A move swaps two neighbours. After exactly 45 moves, can the row be back in its starting order?

choices.misconception: I assumed enough moves can undo anything, without asking what each move preserves.

choices.text: Yes, if the swaps are chosen well
choices.misconception: I tried a few sequences that nearly worked and assumed a better choice would finish the job.

choices.text: No, because 45 is not a multiple of 10
choices.misconception: I reached for the number of items rather than for what a single swap actually changes.

choices.text: No, because the number of moves is odd
It depends which numbers are swapped
choices.misconception: I thought the choice of swaps could change the outcome, when every swap has the same effect.

hints: What does one swap change, whatever you swap?
Count the pairs of numbers standing in the wrong order relative to each other. Work out how one swap of neighbours changes that count - it is always by the same amount.
Swapping two neighbours changes the number of out-of-order pairs by exactly one, so the count flips between odd and even every move. It starts at zero.

solutions.reliable: Count how many pairs of numbers are in the wrong order relative to each other. A swap of two neighbours changes the order of exactly one pair, so this count goes up or down by exactly 1 every move - flipping between odd and even. In the starting row the count is 0, which is even. After 45 moves, an odd number, the count must be odd, so it cannot be 0. The row cannot be back where it started. The transferable idea: find a quantity that every move changes in the same predictable way, and the answer follows without trying anything.
solutions.elegant: Each neighbour swap flips the arrangement's parity, so an odd number of swaps can never return to the arrangement you started from.

problems.whyOnTest: It is the clearest case of a parity argument beating a search, and every distractor is a plausible reason that does not actually work.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: The numbers 1 to 8 are on a board. A move rubs out two of them and writes their difference, larger minus smaller. After seven moves one number is left. Can it be 1?

choices.text: Yes, and there are many ways
choices.misconception: I found sequences ending in small numbers and assumed 1 was among the reachable ones.
I assumed a hard-looking question must have exactly one answer.

choices.text: No, the last number is always even
No, the last number is always 0
choices.misconception: I found one sequence ending in 0 and assumed every sequence must end there.

choices.text: It depends on the order of the moves
choices.misconception: I thought the order could change the outcome, when the quantity that decides it never changes.

hints: Watch what happens to the total.
Add everything on the board and see how one move changes that total. Replacing a and b by their difference always changes it by the same kind of amount.
The total starts at 1 + 2 + ... + 8 = 36, which is even. A move changes the total by twice the smaller number, so it stays even and the last number cannot be odd.

solutions.reliable: Track the total of everything on the board. It starts at 1 + 2 + ... + 8 = 36, which is even. A move replaces a and b with a - b, so the total drops by (a + b) - (a - b) = 2b, always an even amount. The total therefore stays even for ever, and the single number left at the end is that total, so it is even. Since 1 is odd, it can never be the last number. The transferable idea: a quantity no move can change decides the answer before you try anything.
solutions.elegant: Differences preserve parity, so the last number always matches the parity of 1 + 2 + ... + 8, which is even.

problems.whyOnTest: Invariants replace an unbounded search with one observation, and choice D punishes stopping at the first example you happen to find.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A number is doubled, then 6 is added, then the result is halved. The answer is 11. What was the original number?

choices.misconception: I undid the operations in the order they were written instead of in reverse order.
I gave the final answer back, assuming the three steps cancelled each other out.
I doubled the 11 and subtracted the 6 but forgot the final halving that undoes the doubling.
I undid only the halving and stopped there without touching the other two steps.

hints: Start at 11 and undo each step.
Reverse both the operations and their order. The halving happened last, so undo it first, then the addition, then the doubling.
Undo the halving: 11 x 2 = 22. Undo the addition: 22 - 6 = 16. Undo the doubling: 16 divided by 2 = 8.

solutions.reliable: Run the machine backwards. The last step was halving, so undo it first: 11 x 2 = 22. Before the 6 was added it was 22 - 6 = 16. Before doubling it was 16 divided by 2 = 8. Check forwards: 8 doubled is 16, plus 6 is 22, halved is 11. The transferable idea: reverse the operations and the order together, and always check forwards at the end.
solutions.elegant: Doubling and then halving cancel, so the machine is really add 6 then halve, making the start 2 x 11 - 6 all halved: 8.

problems.whyOnTest: Working backwards is worth several marks a paper, and reversing the operations while keeping the original order is the reliable way to get it wrong.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Can a 10 by 10 board be covered exactly by T-shaped tiles of four squares each, with no gaps and no overlaps?

choices.misconception: I checked that 100 divides by 4 and treated that as proof that a covering exists.

choices.text: Yes, but the arrangement is fiddly
choices.misconception: I assumed a covering must exist somewhere and that I simply had not found it yet.

choices.text: No, because 100 is not a multiple of 4
choices.misconception: I gave a reason that is not even true, since 100 really is a multiple of 4.

choices.text: No, because the two colours cannot balance
It depends how the tiles are turned
choices.misconception: I thought orientation could rescue it, but every turn of a T covers the same mixture of colours.

hints: Colour the board like a chessboard.
Count the black and white squares one T-tile covers, whichever way it is turned. Then ask whether twenty-five such tiles can add up to the fifty black squares the board has.
Every T covers either 3 black and 1 white or 1 black and 3 white. With 25 tiles the black total always comes out odd, and 50 is even.

solutions.reliable: Colour the board like a chessboard: 50 black and 50 white squares. However a T-tile is placed, it covers either 3 black and 1 white, or 1 black and 3 white. Suppose k tiles are of the first kind and the other 25 - k of the second. The black squares covered come to 3k + (25 - k) = 2k + 25, which is odd for every whole k, so it can never equal 50. No covering exists. Note that the area check passes, since 100 divides by 4, which is exactly why an area check is not enough. The transferable idea: an area check is necessary and never sufficient; a colouring can rule out what the area allows.
solutions.elegant: Each T covers an odd number of black squares, and twenty-five odd numbers add to an odd total, but the board has an even 50.

problems.whyOnTest: It is the cleanest demonstration that an area check proves nothing, and choice C is the reason a student gives when they have not found the real one.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence starts at 3. Each term after that is double the one before it, minus 1. What is the sixth term?

choices.misconception: I stopped at the fourth term, counting the starting number as the first step rather than the first term.
I generated one term too few, giving the fifth term instead of the sixth.
I doubled six times and subtracted 1 only once at the end.
I generated one term too many, giving the seventh instead of the sixth.

hints: Write the terms out one at a time.
A recursive rule tells you how to get the next term from the last one. There is no formula to jump to - generate the terms in order and count them as you go.
3, then 5, then 9, then 17, then 33, then 65. Counting the starting 3 as the first term, the sixth is 65.

solutions.reliable: Apply the rule term by term, writing each one down and numbering it. Term 1 is 3. Term 2 is 2 x 3 - 1 = 5. Then 2 x 5 - 1 = 9, then 17, then 33, then 65. Counting carefully, the sixth term is 65. The transferable idea: with a recursive rule, number the terms as you write them - almost every error here is being one term out.
solutions.elegant: Each term is one more than a power of two: 3, 5, 9, 17, 33, 65 are 2 to the powers 1 to 6, each plus one.

problems.whyOnTest: Recursive rules cannot be jumped, only generated, and being one term out is by far the most common way to lose the mark.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A sequence starts 1, 1, and every term after that is the sum of the two before it. What is the eighth term?

choices.misconception: I counted the two starting terms as one, so I stopped at the seventh term.
I added the two before it but slipped once in the middle of the chain.
I generated one term too many and gave the ninth.
I doubled each term instead of adding the two before it.

hints: Write the terms in a numbered row.
Each term needs the two before it, so there is no shortcut. Write them across the page with their positions underneath, and read off the one you were asked for.
1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21. The eighth term is 21.

solutions.reliable: Generate the terms and number them: term 1 is 1, term 2 is 1, then 1 + 1 = 2, 1 + 2 = 3, 2 + 3 = 5, 3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 8 = 13, 8 + 13 = 21. The eighth term is 21. The transferable idea: write the position under every term - with two starting values it is very easy to be one out.

problems.whyOnTest: Two starting terms rather than one is exactly what makes students miscount the position, and this sequence appears in some form most years.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A machine turns 3 into 7, 5 into 11 and 8 into 17. What does it turn 12 into?

choices.misconception: I used the rule add 4, which fits the first example but not the others.
I found a rule from two examples only and never tested it against the third.
I doubled the input and forgot the extra one that every example needs.
I used double and add five, which fits none of the examples exactly.

hints: Compare each output with double its input.
Try the simplest families in order: add something, multiply by something, or multiply and then add. Whatever you find has to fit every example, not just the first two.
Double 3 is 6 and the output is 7. Double 5 is 10 and the output is 11. Double 8 is 16 and the output is 17. So the rule is double and add one, giving 25.

solutions.reliable: Test the simple families in order. Adding a fixed amount fails: 3 to 7 is plus 4, but 5 to 11 is plus 6. Try doubling: 3 doubles to 6, one short of 7; 5 doubles to 10, one short of 11; 8 doubles to 16, one short of 17. So the rule is double and add one, and 12 becomes 25. The transferable idea: a candidate rule must fit every example given, and the awkward one is there precisely to kill the wrong rules.

problems.whyOnTest: Several rules fit two examples and only one fits three, so the discipline is testing against all of them before answering.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Dots are arranged in triangles: 1 dot, then 3, then 6, then 10, and so on. How many dots does the tenth triangle have?

choices.misconception: I stopped at the eighth triangle, losing count while adding the rows.
I gave the ninth triangle instead of the tenth, being one row short.
I gave the eleventh triangle, adding one row too many.
I squared the position number, which describes square patterns rather than triangular ones.

hints: What is added from one triangle to the next?
The jumps are not equal: each new triangle adds one more row than the last one added. Write the differences down and you will see the pattern in them.
The differences are 2, 3, 4, 5 and so on, so the tenth triangle is 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 10 = 55.

solutions.reliable: Look at what is added: 1 to 3 adds 2, 3 to 6 adds 3, 6 to 10 adds 4. Each step adds one more than the last, because each new triangle gains a longer bottom row. So the tenth triangle is 1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 10, which pairs up as five lots of 11 = 55. The transferable idea: when the differences themselves form a pattern, add the differences rather than continuing the drawing.
solutions.elegant: The nth triangular number is n times n plus one, halved: 10 x 11 / 2 = 55.

problems.whyOnTest: Growth patterns are the first place a constant difference fails, and noticing that the differences themselves grow is the whole move.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A mother is 32 and her child is 8. In how many years will the mother be exactly three times as old as the child?

choices.misconception: I aged only the child and left the mother's age unchanged.
I looked for when the mother is four times as old rather than three times.
I used the age difference of 24 and halved it, without checking the ratio it gives.
I gave the difference between their ages, which never changes, instead of a number of years.

hints: Age both of them, not just one.
In x years the mother is 32 + x and the child is 8 + x. Write the condition as an equation between those two and solve it. The difference between their ages never changes.
32 + x = 3(8 + x) gives 32 + x = 24 + 3x, so 8 = 2x and x = 4. Check: 36 is three times 12.

solutions.reliable: In x years the mother is 32 + x and the child is 8 + x. The condition is 32 + x = 3(8 + x), which is 32 + x = 24 + 3x, so 8 = 2x and x = 4. Check: in 4 years they are 36 and 12, and 36 is exactly three times 12. The transferable idea: everyone ages at the same rate, so add the same x to every age - and the difference between two ages never changes.
solutions.elegant: The gap is always 24. When the mother is three times as old, the gap is two of the child's ages, so the child is 12 - which is 4 years away.

problems.whyOnTest: Ageing only one person is the classic mistake, and the constant difference is the fact that makes the elegant route possible.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A class of 12 scored an average of 8. Another class of 18 scored an average of 13. What is the average for all 30 students together?

choices.misconception: I averaged the two averages, ignoring that the classes are different sizes.
I weighted the averages but used the wrong class size against each one.
I leaned towards the larger class's average without computing the totals.
I added the two averages together instead of combining them.

hints: Turn both averages into totals.
An average multiplied by its group size gives that group's total. Add the two totals, then divide by the number of students altogether. Never average two averages of different-sized groups.
The totals are 12 x 8 = 96 and 18 x 13 = 234, adding to 330. Then 330 divided by 30 = 11.

solutions.reliable: Turn each average into a total. The first class scored 12 x 8 = 96 and the second 18 x 13 = 234, so together 330 across 30 students. The combined average is 330 divided by 30 = 11. Note it is not 10.5, the average of the two averages - the larger class pulls the result towards 13. The transferable idea: averages of different-sized groups combine through their totals, never by averaging the averages.
solutions.elegant: The classes split 2 to 3, so the answer sits two fifths of the way from 13 to 8: 13 - 2 = 11.

problems.whyOnTest: Averaging the averages is the defining error of weighted-average problems and it produces an answer that looks completely reasonable.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A bag of flour holds 2.5 kg. 1750 g are used. How many grams are left?

choices.misconception: I worked in kilograms and gave the answer in kilograms when grams were asked for.
I converted 2.5 kg to 250 g rather than 2500 g.
I subtracted 1750 from 3000, mis-converting 2.5 kg as three thousand grams.
I subtracted without converting at all, taking 2.5 away from 1750.

hints: Convert to grams before subtracting.
Put both amounts in the same unit first, and check the direction of the conversion by asking whether the number should get bigger or smaller. Then check the unit the answer is wanted in.

solutions.reliable: Convert first: 1 kg is 1000 g, so 2.5 kg is 2500 g - bigger, as it should be. Then subtract in matching units: 2500 - 1750 = 750 g. The answer was asked for in grams, so 750 is the final answer, not 0.75. The transferable idea: convert, then calculate, then check the unit you were asked for.

problems.whyOnTest: Two unit traps in one question - the conversion and the answer's unit - and both are the kind that cost a mark on a question the student can do.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: One pipe fills a pool in 12 hours and another fills it in 4 hours. With both running, how many hours does the pool take to fill?

choices.misconception: I gave the faster pipe's time on its own, forgetting the slower one helps as well.
I halved the slower pipe's time rather than adding the two rates.
I averaged the two times, which would only be right if the pipes took turns.
I added the two times, which makes two pipes slower than one - an impossible answer.

hints: How much does each pipe fill in an hour?
Work in pools per hour rather than hours per pool. Add the two hourly amounts to get the pair's rate, then turn that back into a time.
In an hour the pipes fill one twelfth and one quarter, which is one twelfth plus three twelfths = four twelfths, or a third. So 3 hours.

solutions.reliable: Switch to rates. In one hour the first pipe fills 1/12 of the pool and the second fills 1/4 = 3/12. Together they fill 4/12 = 1/3 of the pool per hour, so the whole pool takes 3 hours. Sanity check: two pipes must beat the faster pipe alone, and 3 is less than 4. The transferable idea: add rates, never times - and check the answer beats the faster worker on its own.
solutions.elegant: The second pipe is three times as fast as the first, so together they work at four times the first pipe's rate: 12 divided by 4 = 3 hours.

problems.whyOnTest: Adding the times gives an answer slower than one pipe alone, and noticing that absurdity is itself the lesson.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A train covers 150 km at a steady 60 km per hour. How many minutes does the journey take?

choices.misconception: I divided 150 by 60 and read the answer as minutes rather than hours.
I used 1.5 hours instead of 2.5, dividing 90 by 60 rather than 150.
I converted 2.5 hours as two hours and fifty minutes.
I multiplied the distance by 60 instead of dividing, then converted.

hints: Find the time in hours first.
Time is distance divided by speed, which gives an answer in hours. Convert to minutes only at the end, and check the size of the number after converting.
150 divided by 60 is 2.5 hours, and 2.5 x 60 = 150 minutes.

solutions.reliable: Time is distance divided by speed: 150 divided by 60 = 2.5 hours. The question asks for minutes, so convert at the end: 2.5 x 60 = 150 minutes. It is a coincidence that the answer in minutes matches the distance in kilometres, which is exactly why the working matters more than the number. The transferable idea: compute in the natural unit, convert last, and check the answer's size after converting.

problems.whyOnTest: A coincidence between two numbers in the question makes it easy to arrive at the right answer for the wrong reason, and the unit conversion is the real test.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Everyone at a meeting shakes hands with everyone else exactly once. There are 66 handshakes in total. How many people are there?

choices.misconception: I used the number of hands each person shakes rather than the number of people.
I doubled the answer, forgetting that the halving has already been done.
I halved 66 and treated that as the number of people.
I gave the number of handshakes back as the number of people.

hints: Try 3 people, then 4, then 5.
Work out the handshakes for a few small groups and write the results in a list. The pattern that appears lets you climb to 66 without any algebra.
3 people give 3 handshakes, 4 give 6, 5 give 10. The counts are 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55, 66 - and 66 is reached at 12 people.

solutions.reliable: Try small cases and list the results. With 3 people there are 3 handshakes, with 4 there are 6, with 5 there are 10. Continuing: 15, 21, 28, 36, 45, 55, 66. Counting along, 66 handshakes happens with 12 people. Check: each of 12 shakes 11 hands, giving 132 ends, and each handshake has two ends: 66. The transferable idea: small cases turn a question you cannot start into a list you can read the answer off.
solutions.elegant: n people give n(n - 1)/2 handshakes, so n(n - 1) = 132 = 12 x 11, giving n = 12.

problems.whyOnTest: Starting small is the single most reliable way into a question that looks like it needs algebra a student has not met yet.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these numbers has exactly 6 different whole-number factors, counting 1 and the number itself?

choices.misconception: I assumed a number with two different prime factors always has six factors.
I counted the factors of 16 as six by including a number twice.
I assumed a square number has six factors without listing them.
I counted the powers of 3 up to 27 and thought there were six of them.

hints: List the factors of each choice in pairs.
The answer is one of the five, so testing beats deriving. For each one, list its factors in pairs that multiply to the number - the pairing stops you missing any.
12 pairs up as 1 and 12, 2 and 6, 3 and 4: six factors. 15 has four, 16 has five, 25 has three, 27 has four.

solutions.reliable: Test each choice by listing its factors in pairs. 12: 1 x 12, 2 x 6, 3 x 4 - six factors. 15: 1 x 15, 3 x 5 - four. 16: 1 x 16, 2 x 8, 4 x 4 - five, because 4 pairs with itself. 25: 1 x 25, 5 x 5 - three. 27: 1 x 27, 3 x 9 - four. Only 12 has six. The transferable idea: on a multiple-choice paper, testing five candidates is often faster than finding a rule, and pairing the factors makes each test quick and safe.

problems.whyOnTest: Back-solving beats deriving here, and pairing factors is what stops a square number being miscounted.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangle has an area of 36 and sides that are whole numbers. Which of these could NOT be its perimeter?

choices.misconception: I ruled out the square 6 by 6, forgetting that a square is a rectangle.
I did not think to try 4 by 9, so I judged this perimeter impossible.
I missed the 3 by 12 rectangle when listing the factor pairs.
I stopped listing factor pairs before reaching 2 by 18.

hints: List every factor pair of 36.
Whole-number sides with area 36 means the sides are a factor pair of 36. List all the pairs, work out each perimeter, and see which offered value never appears.
The pairs are 1 and 36, 2 and 18, 3 and 12, 4 and 9, 6 and 6, giving perimeters 74, 40, 30, 26 and 24. There is no 28.

solutions.reliable: Whole-number sides multiplying to 36 must be a factor pair. The pairs are 1 x 36, 2 x 18, 3 x 12, 4 x 9 and 6 x 6, giving perimeters of 74, 40, 30, 26 and 24. Every offered value appears except 28, so 28 is impossible. The transferable idea: bounding and listing the possibilities rules choices out far faster than trying to construct the awkward one.
solutions.elegant: A perimeter of 28 needs sides adding to 14 and multiplying to 36, and no pair of whole numbers does both.

problems.whyOnTest: Ruling choices out by what is possible is a different skill from computing an answer, and it is the one a could-not question demands.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these is closest to the number of seconds in one day?

choices.misconception: I gave the number of minutes in a day instead of the number of seconds.
I gave the number of seconds in one hour rather than in a whole day.
I multiplied the 24 hours by a round thousand instead of converting properly.
I multiplied 60 by a round thousand, using one conversion and inventing the other.

hints: Go hours, then minutes, then seconds.
Convert one step at a time and check the size after each step. Because the choices are far apart, a rough calculation is enough to pick the right one.
24 hours is 24 x 60 = 1440 minutes, and 1440 x 60 = 86400 seconds.

solutions.reliable: Convert in stages. A day is 24 hours, which is 24 x 60 = 1440 minutes, which is 1440 x 60 = 86 400 seconds. Even roughly: 1400 x 60 is about 84 000, which already separates the choices decisively. The transferable idea: when the choices are far apart, a rough calculation picks the answer and costs a fraction of the time.

problems.whyOnTest: Widely spaced choices are an invitation to estimate, and every wrong choice here is the answer to a different, easier question.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

choices.misconception: I cancelled the chain but stopped one factor early, leaving a 9 on the bottom.
I worked out the first bracket and assumed the rest made no difference.
I gave the last bracket on its own instead of the whole product.
I assumed everything cancels completely, leaving nothing behind.

hints: Write each bracket as a single fraction.
Turn every bracket into one fraction before multiplying anything. Then write the whole product out in a line and look at what appears on the top and on the bottom.
The brackets are 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, ... , 9/10. Every top cancels the bottom before it, leaving 1 on top and 10 underneath.

solutions.reliable: Write each bracket as one fraction: 1 - 1/2 is 1/2, 1 - 1/3 is 2/3, 1 - 1/4 is 3/4, and so on up to 9/10. The product is (1 x 2 x 3 x ... x 9) over (2 x 3 x 4 x ... x 10). Everything cancels except the 1 on top and the 10 underneath, giving 1/10. Grinding it out multiplication by multiplication gives the same answer and takes ten times as long. The transferable idea: rewrite before you calculate - the shortcut only becomes visible once the terms are in a comparable form.
solutions.elegant: Each bracket is (k - 1)/k, so the product telescopes to 1/10 whatever the last denominator is.

problems.whyOnTest: It is the clearest case of a problem that is two minutes of grinding or fifteen seconds of noticing, and the decision between the two is the skill.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: You are 20 minutes into a 75-minute paper of 30 questions, still on question 9, and four minutes in with no progress. What is the best move?

choices.text: Keep going — four minutes are already invested
choices.misconception: I let the time already spent decide, but that time is gone whatever I do next.

choices.text: Answer it with your best guess, mark it, and move on
Skip it, leave it blank, and come back at the end
choices.misconception: I moved on but left a blank, which scores nothing if I never get back to it.

choices.text: Go back and re-check questions 1 to 8
choices.misconception: I spent time re-reading work I had no reason to doubt, while 21 unseen questions waited.

choices.text: Jump to question 30 and work backwards
choices.misconception: I assumed the hardest questions are the best use of time, when the unseen easy ones are worth the same each.

hints: The four minutes are gone either way.
Ask what the next minute is worth, not what the last four cost. There are 21 questions you have not read, and a blank scores nothing while a guess costs nothing.
Guess, mark it to revisit, and move on. That banks a chance of a mark, costs nothing if wrong, and frees the time for questions you have not even seen.

solutions.reliable: Time already spent cannot be recovered, so it should not affect the decision. What matters is what the next minute buys: on question 9 it buys another attempt at something that has resisted four minutes; on question 10 it buys a fresh question worth the same marks. Guessing first is what makes moving on free - Kangaroo deducts nothing for a wrong answer, so a filled bubble is never worse than a blank one, and marking it means you can return if time allows. The transferable idea: guess, mark, move - in that order, because the guess is what protects you if you never come back.

problems.whyOnTest: Triage decides more marks than any single technique, and letting invested time drive the choice is the bias that costs the most.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A rectangle measures 30 cm by 0.4 m. What is its area in square centimetres?

choices.misconception: I worked entirely in metres and gave the answer in square metres.
I multiplied 30 by 0.4 without converting the metres to centimetres at all.
I converted 0.4 m to 4 cm rather than 40 cm.
I converted 0.4 m to 400 cm, moving the decimal point one place too far.

hints: Put both sides in the same unit first.
Convert before multiplying, and check the direction: metres to centimetres makes the number bigger. Then check the unit the answer is wanted in before writing it down.
0.4 m is 40 cm, so the area is 30 x 40 = 1200 square centimetres.

solutions.reliable: Convert first: 0.4 m is 0.4 x 100 = 40 cm - bigger, as changing to a smaller unit should be. Then the area is 30 x 40 = 1200 square centimetres. Check the unit asked for: square centimetres, which is what we have. The transferable idea: convert, calculate, then re-read the units in the question before writing the answer down.

problems.whyOnTest: Two of the five choices are right numbers in wrong units, which is exactly how this mark is lost in a real paper.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Work out 17 x 24, then check it a second way before you commit to an answer.

choices.misconception: I worked out 17 times 20 and forgot to add the 17 times 4 part.
I worked out 17 times 4 as 28 instead of 68 when adding the parts together.
I worked out 17 times 4 as 48 instead of 68 when adding the parts together.
I made a carrying slip of ten in the final addition of the two parts.

hints: Do it once, then check it a different way.
Split 24 into 20 and 4 and add the two products. Then check by a different route, such as 17 times 25 minus 17, rather than reading your own working again.

solutions.reliable: Split the 24: 17 x 20 = 340 and 17 x 4 = 68, so the total is 340 + 68 = 408. Now check by a genuinely different route rather than re-reading: 17 x 25 is a quarter of 1700, which is 425, and 24 is one less than 25, so subtract one 17 to get 425 - 17 = 408. Two different methods agreeing is worth far more than reading the same working twice, because rereading repeats the same mistake. The transferable idea: check with a different method, not with the same one again.
solutions.elegant: 17 x 24 is 17 x 25 minus 17, and a quarter of 1700 is 425, so the answer is 408.

problems.whyOnTest: Every wrong choice here is a real arithmetic slip that rereading your own working would not catch, but a second method would.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: You reach the ten 5-point questions with 18 minutes left. What is the best plan?

choices.text: Start at the first and work through in order until time runs out
choices.misconception: I worked in order, so a hard early question could eat the time meant for easier later ones.

choices.text: Read all ten quickly, pick the two or three that look most doable, and fill in every answer before the end
Spend the whole time on the last question, since it is the hardest
choices.misconception: I assumed the hardest question is worth the most, but every question in this block scores the same.

choices.text: Answer the ones with the shortest statements
choices.misconception: I used length as a proxy for difficulty, which is not reliable in this block.

choices.text: Divide the time evenly, about 1.8 minutes each
choices.misconception: I spread the time equally, which is too little for the questions I could do and wasted on the ones I could not.

hints: Every question in this block scores the same.
Ten questions at the same value means the aim is to maximise how many you finish, not to conquer the hardest. Spend the first ninety seconds finding out which ones are yours.
Read all ten first, pick the two or three you can genuinely do, work those properly, and fill in a guess on the rest before the end.

solutions.reliable: Every question in this block is worth 5 points, so a hard one is worth no more than an easy one. The plan that maximises marks is therefore: spend the first ninety seconds reading all ten and marking the ones that look tractable; work those properly, because a half-finished 5-point question scores the same as an untouched one; and before the end, fill in an answer for every remaining question, since blanks score nothing and wrong answers cost nothing. The transferable idea: with equal-value questions, the aim is how many you finish, not how hard the ones you attempt are.

problems.whyOnTest: The 5-point block is where the paper is won or lost, and working strictly in order is the plan that leaves the most marks on the table.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which of these fractions lies between one third and one half?

choices.misconception: I compared the bottom numbers and assumed a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction.
I saw that 4 lies between 3 and 2 and assumed one quarter therefore lies between the two fractions.
I checked that it is bigger than one third but never checked it against one half.
I compared the top numbers only and ignored what the bottoms do to the size.

hints: Turn them all into decimals.
One third is about 0.33 and one half is 0.5. Convert each choice to a decimal and see which one lands strictly between those two numbers.
1/5 is 0.2, 1/4 is 0.25, 2/5 is 0.4, 3/5 is 0.6, 2/3 is about 0.67. Only 0.4 sits between 0.33 and 0.5.

solutions.reliable: Convert everything to decimals so they can be compared on one scale. One third is about 0.33 and one half is 0.5. The choices are 0.2, 0.25, 0.4, 0.6 and about 0.67. Only 0.4, which is two fifths, lies strictly between 0.33 and 0.5. The transferable idea: put fractions on a common footing - decimals or a common denominator - before comparing, because a bigger denominator makes a fraction smaller, not larger.
solutions.elegant: Over fifteenths, one third is 5/15 and one half is 7.5/15, and two fifths is 6/15 - comfortably between them.

problems.whyOnTest: Comparing fractions by looking at one number at a time is the most persistent misconception in the number strand.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Which capital letter, printed plainly, has both a horizontal and a vertical line of symmetry?

choices.misconception: I found the vertical fold and assumed a horizontal one must work too.
I found the horizontal fold and stopped without testing the vertical one.
I counted the vertical fold twice rather than testing a horizontal one.
I mistook turning the letter upside down for folding it, which is rotation rather than symmetry about a line.

hints: Fold each letter twice: across, then down.
Test both folds separately on every letter. A letter passes only if the two halves land exactly on each other for the horizontal fold and for the vertical fold.
A and T fold vertically only. B folds horizontally only. Z looks the same upside down but has no fold at all. H folds both ways.

solutions.reliable: Test both folds on each letter. A folds along a vertical line but not a horizontal one. B folds horizontally but not vertically. T folds vertically only. Z has no line of symmetry at all - it looks the same when turned half a turn, which is rotation, not reflection. H folds along both its vertical and its horizontal midline. The transferable idea: looking the same after a turn is not the same as having a line of symmetry, and choice E is exactly that confusion.

problems.whyOnTest: Confusing rotational symmetry with a line of symmetry is a distinct, common error, and Z is the letter that exposes it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: How many three-digit numbers can be written using only the digits 1 and 2, with repeats allowed?

choices.misconception: I counted the two available digits rather than the numbers they can build.
I counted the three positions instead of the numbers.
I used only two of the three positions when multiplying.
I multiplied 2 by 3, mixing the number of digits with the number of positions.

hints: Two choices in each of three positions.
Each position independently takes one of two digits, and using a digit does not use it up. Multiply the options position by position rather than adding them.

solutions.reliable: Each of the three positions can hold either digit, and repeats are allowed so nothing gets used up. That gives 2 x 2 x 2 = 8. Listing confirms it: 111, 112, 121, 122, 211, 212, 221, 222. The transferable idea: independent choices multiply, and the number of positions is an exponent, not a factor to multiply the digits by.

problems.whyOnTest: Multiplying the digit count by the position count instead of raising it to that power is the standard slip, and choice D is exactly it.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Three more than twice a number is 19. What is the number?

choices.misconception: I subtracted 8 from 19 rather than working the two steps backwards.
I subtracted the 3 from 19 and gave that without halving it.
I added the 3 to 19 instead of subtracting it.
I doubled 19 and added 3, applying the machine forwards instead of undoing it.

hints: Undo the last step first.
The number was doubled and then 3 was added. To go backwards, take the 3 off first and then halve - the reverse operations in the reverse order.
19 - 3 = 16, and 16 divided by 2 = 8. Check: twice 8 is 16, plus 3 is 19.

solutions.reliable: Write what happened: the number was doubled, then 3 was added, giving 19. Undo in reverse: 19 - 3 = 16, then 16 divided by 2 = 8. Check forwards: 2 x 8 + 3 = 19. The transferable idea: reverse both the operations and their order, and always check by running it forwards again.

problems.whyOnTest: Three more than twice a number puts the operations in the opposite order to the words, which is where the translation goes wrong.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: A counter sits at the point (3, 5) on a grid. It moves 4 squares right and 2 squares down. Where is it now?

choices.misconception: I moved left instead of right, subtracting the 4 rather than adding it.
I moved left and up, reversing both directions.
I swapped the two coordinates round before moving.
I moved up instead of down, adding the 2 rather than subtracting it.

hints: Across changes the first number, up changes the second.
The first coordinate is how far across and the second is how far up. Right adds to the first, down subtracts from the second. Change them one at a time.
Moving 4 right takes 3 to 7. Moving 2 down takes 5 to 3. So the counter is at (7, 3).

solutions.reliable: The first number says how far across, the second how far up. Moving 4 squares right adds 4 to the first: 3 + 4 = 7. Moving 2 squares down subtracts 2 from the second: 5 - 2 = 3. So the counter is at (7, 3). The transferable idea: change one coordinate at a time and say the direction out loud - right adds, left subtracts, up adds, down subtracts.

problems.whyOnTest: Swapping the coordinates or the sign of a direction accounts for almost every lost mark on grid questions.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Suppose it is true that some birds cannot fly. Which of these must also be true?

choices.misconception: I read some cannot as meaning none can, which is a far stronger claim.
I chose a statement that directly contradicts the one I was given.
I read some as meaning a majority, when it only guarantees at least one.
I read some as meaning exactly one, when it means at least one.

hints: How few birds could some be?
Some means at least one, and nothing more. Test each choice against the smallest situation the statement allows: exactly one bird in the whole world that cannot fly.
If exactly one bird cannot fly, then it is false that all birds can fly - but every other choice would also have to be false.

solutions.reliable: Some means at least one, and no more than that. Test each choice against the case where exactly one bird cannot fly and every other bird can. No birds can fly is false there. All birds can fly is false there. Most birds cannot fly is false there. Exactly one bird cannot fly happens to be true there but would be false if two birds could not fly, so it is not guaranteed. Not all birds can fly is true in every case allowed by the statement. The transferable idea: to test must be true, find the weakest situation the statement allows and check each choice against it.
solutions.elegant: Some A are not B is precisely the negation of all A are B, so the two are equivalent and nothing stronger follows.

problems.whyOnTest: Some, most and all are read interchangeably by students under time pressure, and every wrong choice here is one of those readings.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: Two circles touch on the outside. One has a radius of 3 cm and the other a radius of 5 cm. How many centimetres apart are their centres?

choices.misconception: I subtracted the radii, which is the answer when one circle sits inside the other.
I averaged the two radii instead of adding them.
I multiplied the radii together rather than adding them.
I added the two diameters instead of the two radii.

hints: Draw the line joining the two centres.
Draw a straight line from one centre to the other. It passes through the point where the circles touch, so it is made of one radius from each circle, laid end to end.
The line from centre to centre is 3 + 5 = 8 cm.

solutions.reliable: Draw the line joining the two centres. Because the circles touch on the outside, that line passes through the single point where they meet, so it is exactly one radius of the first circle plus one radius of the second: 3 + 5 = 8 cm. If instead one circle sat inside the other and touched, the distance would be the difference, 5 - 3 = 2 - which is choice A. The transferable idea: joining the centres turns a circle question into a length question.

problems.whyOnTest: Touching on the outside and touching on the inside give the sum and the difference of the radii, and the two are constantly confused.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the smaller angle between the hands of a clock at exactly 4 o'clock?

choices.misconception: I gave the angle for a single hour mark rather than the four marks between the hands.
I counted two hour marks instead of four.
I assumed any gap of a few hours is a right angle, as it is at three o'clock.
I measured the angle the long way round the clock face instead of the smaller one.

hints: One hour mark is how many degrees?
The twelve hour marks share 360 degrees between them. Work out what one mark is worth, count the marks between the two hands, and take the smaller of the two ways round.
One mark is 360 divided by 12 = 30 degrees. At 4 o'clock the hands are 4 marks apart, so 4 x 30 = 120 degrees.

solutions.reliable: The twelve hour marks divide 360 degrees, so each mark is 30 degrees. At exactly 4 o'clock the minute hand points at 12 and the hour hand at 4, which is 4 marks apart. That is 4 x 30 = 120 degrees. Going the other way round would be 240, so the smaller angle is 120. The transferable idea: fix the 30-degrees-per-mark fact once and every clock question becomes a multiplication - then check which way round the question wants.
solutions.elegant: Four hours is a third of the clock face, and a third of 360 is 120.

problems.whyOnTest: The 30-degrees-per-mark fact plus the which-way-round check is the whole of clock geometry at this level.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi

problems.statement: What is the units digit of 3 multiplied by itself 100 times, that is 3 to the power 100?

choices.misconception: I assumed every power of 3 ends in 3.
I found the cycle 3, 9, 7, 1 but counted its positions from zero, landing one step early.
I used a remainder of 2 instead of 0 when dividing 100 by the cycle length of 4.

choices.text: it cannot be found without a calculator
choices.misconception: I assumed a number this large has no reachable last digit, rather than looking for a repeat.

hints: List the last digits of the first few powers.
The last digit of a product depends only on the last digits being multiplied. Work out the last digits of the first few powers until the list repeats, then locate 100 inside that cycle.
The last digits run 3, 9, 7, 1 and then repeat. 100 divides exactly by 4, so it lands on the last entry of a cycle, which is 1.

solutions.reliable: Build the cycle of last digits: 3, then 9, then 27 ends in 7, then 81 ends in 1, then it starts again at 3. The cycle has length 4. Now 100 divided by 4 is 25 with remainder 0, and a remainder of 0 means the last entry of a cycle, not the first - so the answer is 1. The transferable idea: find the cycle, then use the remainder as a position inside it, remembering that remainder zero lands at the end.
solutions.elegant: 3 to the power 4 is 81, which ends in 1, and 100 is a multiple of 4 - so the answer ends in 1.

problems.whyOnTest: The remainder-of-zero case is the one students get wrong, and choices C and D are the two ways of being one step out.
problems.author: Devansh Sanghavi
